title: The Bell That Wasn't There
subtitle: A Calling With No Ship at the End of It

setting.name: The Sharrow Reef and the Grey Sounding
setting.description: The Grey Sounding is the deep channel running the length of the chain's spine, where warm current meets cold water and lays fog over sixty miles of it for weeks at a time. A vessel crosses it by going from one bell-buoy to the next, listening — bronze carries where light does not — and the buoys are maintained, charted and trusted absolutely, because there is no alternative. Two-thirds of the way down the Sounding lies the Sharrow: a reef of black rock two miles long that never quite breaks except at the bottom of a spring tide, with a charted buoy at its northern end warning vessels off. There are eleven wrecks on the Sharrow. Nine of them are less than three years old, and every one of them has been stripped clean of anything worth carrying away, down to the fastenings.
setting.atmosphere: Fog you can taste. A visible world of about sixty yards in every direction and an audible world of miles. Everything in this scenario is heard before it is seen and half of what is heard is a lie. Beneath the surface the Sharrow is a bright, cold, extraordinarily beautiful place full of ruined ships and unhurried fish, and the horror of it is entirely in the arithmetic: nine hulls in three years on a reef that killed one a decade for the previous century, and someone has been down here with a wrecking-bar on every single one of them.

keyLocations.name: The Northern Sharrow Buoy
keyLocations.description: A charted bell-buoy at the reef's northern end, riding a hundred-fathom chain to a stone sinker, tolling on the swell. It has been on this station for sixty years. It is not where the chart says it is, it is not tolling the pattern it is supposed to toll, and the bell inside its cage is not the bell that was hung there.
features: A cast-iron cage, weed-fouled and barnacled, containing a bronze bell on a swinging clapper-frame
A hundred fathoms of chain running down into green water to a sinker that is nowhere near the charted position
Fresh paint on the cage — three months old at most, and nobody has painted a Sounding buoy in eleven years because the funds ran out
encounters: Getting a boat alongside a working buoy in a swell, which is genuinely difficult and has killed people
Reading the bell, which requires getting inside the cage
The buoy's own signal pattern, which is wrong in a way that only somebody who knows the Sounding will catch
secrets: The bell is recast bronze. Half a stolen harbour's mark survives on the inside of the crown where the recasting did not take: a bell from the Windward Beads hamlet of Nethercombe, whose harbour bell went missing two years ago and was written off as theft for the metal
The sinker has been moved. The chain has been re-shackled at some point in the last three months, and the new shackle is not chain-work — it is smith's work, done ashore

keyLocations.name: The Reef Itself
keyLocations.description: Two miles of black rock lying three to eleven fathoms under, with a spine that dries at the bottom of a spring tide and a maze of gullies and overhangs to seaward. Eleven wrecks lie along it in various states. Nine are recent. In good light and slack water it is one of the most beautiful places in the campaign.
features: Eleven identifiable wrecks: two ancient and grown over, nine within the last three years and all stripped
Gullies and swim-throughs, cold, at three to eleven fathoms — reachable by held breath at the shallow end and by nothing the party owns at the deep end
A working population of reef sharks, giant octopuses and an extremely large moray that has taken up residence in a stern-post
encounters: Diving the wrecks, which is an exhaustion and breath-holding problem before it is anything else
A pair of reef sharks that are not hunting the party but are extremely interested in them
A giant octopus in the wreck of the Charity Bell, which is not hostile until something is taken from its den
secrets: Every one of the nine recent wrecks has been stripped with the same tools in the same order: fastenings first, then instruments, then cargo. That is not opportunistic scavenging. That is a crew with a method and a list
Three of the nine are entered in the ledger at the Hall as having been abandoned by a passing vessel that heard the calling and did not answer. One of those three entries names the Widow's Compass

keyLocations.name: The Wreck of the Charity Bell
keyLocations.description: The most recent of the nine: a Beads-registered ketch, seven months down, lying on her side in four fathoms with her rig still attached and her hatches open. She is the party's best evidence and their worst hour.
features: Hatches opened from outside and left open — a sinking ship's hatches are shut
Every metal fastening above the turn of the bilge cut out with a bar, cleanly, in a numbered sequence
The master's slate still hanging in the companionway, with a course and a time chalked on it and the water having taken everything else
encounters: The dive itself: four fathoms, cold, with a swell working the wreck
The giant octopus resident in the after cabin, which will defend its den and nothing else
What is in the forepeak, which the DM should not describe until a player goes in there
secrets: The slate reads a course and a bearing to the northern Sharrow buoy, timed at four hours before the ketch went down. She was navigating to the buoy. The buoy is what killed her
Four of her people are still aboard, in the forepeak, where they went to get away from the water. Article Six applies to them and the crew of the Widow's Compass will insist on it

keyLocations.name: The Edge of Ossary Deep
keyLocations.description: Where the Sharrow's seaward face falls away into the Grey Sounding proper and the water goes from green to a blue so dark it reads as black. Something down there has been watching the reef for two years, keeping its own count of the ships and of the vessels that came afterwards with bars.
features: A drop-off from eleven fathoms to well over a hundred within twenty yards
Bronze tones coming up out of the deep water, patterned, at intervals — not a buoy, and not random
A line of small bronze markers set into the reef's face at the drop, recently placed, in no chart anywhere
encounters: First contact with the quiet folk of Ossary Deep, on their terms and at their choosing
A conversation that is largely incomprehensible and entirely comprehensible at the same time
Ledda, who comes up out of a hundred fathoms to look at the party and decides something about them
secrets: The quiet folk have watched every one of the nine wrecks happen. They have watched the salvors come afterwards. They keep a count, in bronze, on the reef face, and it is not nine — it is fourteen, because five of the ships they watched die were never found and never entered in any ledger
They were never asked. Not by the Reckoners, not by any master, not once in two years. This is not a puzzle for the party to solve; it is the point, and it should land as an accusation

synopsis: A calling comes up out of the fog in the Grey Sounding and the Widow's Compass answers it, because that is what the Articles say and what the ledger requires — and there is no ship at the end of it. There is a reef, in the wrong place relative to the buoy that is supposed to warn ships off it, and the party very nearly joins the eleven wrecks already lying on it. What they find when they go back and take the buoy apart is a bell of recast bronze still carrying half the mark of a stolen harbour bell, a reef stripped clean by people with a method, and a ledger entry at the Hall blaming one of the wrecks on the Widow's Compass. What they find when they dive it is four people in a forepeak and a deepwater nation that has been keeping a more accurate count than the Reckoners for two years and was never once asked.
hook: The fog in the Grey Sounding has been down for nine days and you have been going buoy to buoy, listening, for two of them, and it is the most tiring kind of sailing there is. At about the fourth hour of the morning watch Sefi Nightjar puts her head over the rail and says 'bell', and everybody stops. Three strokes, a pause, two strokes: a calling, close, and off the starboard bow where there should be nothing at all for eleven miles. Marda Kell has the chart out before anybody says anything and her finger is on a piece of white water that has no business being anywhere near the sound, and she says the thing that will run under the rest of this entire campaign: 'That's not where a bell should be.'

articlesAtStake.note: The party answers a calling that turns out to be a trap. Article One says every hand answers a bell — it does not say every bell is honest, and this scenario is where the crew first has to sit with that.

There is a great deal of loose salvage on the Sharrow and some of it is worth real money to a ship that is nine marks down and cannot get credit. Somebody aboard will be tempted to take before the count.

Four dead in the forepeak of the Charity Bell, seven months down. Naming and ringing out four strangers costs the party the best part of a day on a reef in fog. The crew will not consider that a question.

acts.title: Act 1: A Calling in the Fog
acts.description: The Widow's Compass answers a bell in the Grey Sounding, finds nothing at the end of it but rock, and gets off the Sharrow by seamanship and luck. This act is a near-disaster played straight, and it ends with the party alive, badly frightened, and holding a question.
objectives: Hear and answer the calling in fog with no visibility
Realise, too late, that the ship is inside the reef and not outside it
Get the Widow's Compass off the Sharrow without losing her
Establish that the buoy is not where the chart says it is

scenes.name: Three Strokes and Two
scenes.description: The calling comes out of the fog and the party turns toward it. Everything about this scene should feel like doing the right thing competently.
scenes.readAloud: "Nine days of fog does something to a crew. Nobody has seen more than sixty yards since the Beads and the whole world has shrunk to a wet grey circle with your own ship in the middle of it, and you navigate by listening — buoy to buoy down the Sounding, bronze to bronze, counting the strokes. Then at the fourth hour of the morning watch it comes out of the grey off the starboard bow, close enough that you feel it in the deck: three strokes, a pause, two strokes. A calling. Somebody's in trouble and they are within a mile of you. And Marda Kell has the chart up under the binnacle light with her finger on it, and she is not saying 'put the helm up,' which is what she ought to be saying. She is saying, 'That's not where a bell should be.'"

skillChecks.success: Dead reckoning against the last buoy and the log gives you a position, and the position says there is nothing where that bell is except the northern end of the Sharrow. Something is wrong before you are committed, and you have perhaps four minutes to act on it.
skillChecks.failure: Fog, a wet chart and a nine-day-old fix. You are where you think you are, more or less, and the bell is where the bell is.

skillChecks.success: The pattern is wrong. Not the calling — the buoy underneath it. A Sounding buoy tolls on the swell with a long irregular note and this one is tolling evenly, like something being struck by a hand. Yevet Ourim will say so if no player does.
skillChecks.failure: Bronze in fog is bronze in fog. It sounds like every other bell you have ever heard.

skillChecks.success: Whatever Marda Kell is about to say, she has already decided you are going to overrule her, and she is going to do the thing correctly anyway. That is worth knowing about your sailing master.
skillChecks.failure: She is being difficult about a bell in the middle of the night.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The party should answer. Article One says so, the ledger requires it, and every instinct the first scenario built points that way — and that is exactly why this is the right place to break it. Do not warn them off harder than the checks above allow. If they refuse to answer on a hunch and later prove the bell was false, that is a legitimate and clever outcome: no mark is entered because no vessel was in distress, and the crew is deeply unsettled by a captain who ignores bells on instinct. Crew Regard -1 for the refusal, +2 when the proof arrives.

scenes.name: Inside the Reef
scenes.description: The Widow's Compass is not standing off the Sharrow. She is inside it, in the gullies at its northern end, in fog, with the tide setting her down onto rock. This is the scenario's first crisis and it is pure seamanship.
scenes.readAloud: "The lead comes up at eleven fathoms and then at seven and then the man on the chains says 'four!' in a voice that goes right through the ship, and everybody's stomach drops at once, because four fathoms is less water than the Compass draws when she rolls. Then the fog thins for about two seconds — the way it does, meanly, when it is too late to be useful — and there is black rock forty yards to leeward with the swell standing up on it in slow white walls, and more of it ahead, and more of it inshore, and the bell is still going, three and two, three and two, from somewhere you cannot see. You are not off the Sharrow. You are in it."

skillChecks.success: Every hand who can haul gets on the braces and the yards come round in about nine seconds, which is very good work indeed, and the ship comes up and claws off.
skillChecks.failure: The yards come round late. The Compass touches — a long grinding stagger through the whole hull — and comes off again with two feet of water in her and a plank sprung forward. The pumps are manned every watch for the rest of the scenario and every character on deck takes 1d6 bludgeoning going over.

skillChecks.success: You keep the lead going through all of it and call the water in time, twice, which is the only reason the ship finds the gully she came in by.
skillChecks.failure: The lead-line fouls and there are ninety seconds where nobody aboard knows how much water is under the keel.

skillChecks.success: You read the set of the swell on the rock and take the ship out the way the water is going instead of the way the compass says, which is counter-intuitive, correct, and saves the ship.
skillChecks.failure: You get her out by main strength and good luck rather than good judgement, which works, and everybody knows the difference.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Nothing attacks the ship. This is a navigation emergency and it should be terrifying without a single enemy in it. Let the crew be superb: Marda Kell is worth three officers in this scene, Sefi Nightjar goes up the mast in fog to look for water-colour, Grull Ashpike gets the hands on the braces before anyone orders it. If the ship touches, that damage is real and persists — it is the direct cause of needing a careening yard in bw-scenario-003 and the DM should say so plainly at the time.

scenes.name: Nothing at the End of It
scenes.description: The fog lifts at noon and there is no ship. There has never been a ship. There is a reef, eleven wrecks visible through clear water, and a buoy tolling steadily in the wrong place.
scenes.readAloud: "The fog goes off at noon the way it does out here, all at once, like a sheet coming off furniture, and the Grey Sounding turns out to be a flat blue plain in bright sun with the Sharrow lying black across two miles of it. There is no ship in distress. There is no ship at all. There is the reef, and the water over it is so clear that from the maintop Sefi can count the wrecks on it, and she does, out loud, in a voice that gets flatter with each one: 'Two old ones, all grown over. And then — that's three. Four. Five, six, that's two together. Seven. Eight. Nine.' A pause. 'Captain, they're new. They've all got their paint on.'"

skillChecks.success: From the deck with a glass you can already see the pattern: the nine new wrecks have all been opened. Hatches off, decks broken into, and on two of them the copper is gone off the bottom where it shows above water at low tide.
skillChecks.failure: Nine wrecks. Wrecks look like wrecks from four hundred yards.

skillChecks.success: The Sharrow has a reputation and it is not this one. It has taken about one ship a decade for a century, which is what a well-buoyed reef in a well-known channel ought to take. Nine in three years is not a reef. It is a business.
skillChecks.failure: A bad reef is a bad reef. Sailors have always died on rocks.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the hinge of the campaign and the scene where the premise stops being about a debt and starts being about a crime. Give the players the count from the maintop and then let them sit in it. Anselm Coyle the bell-priest should be visibly, quietly destroyed by this, because a false bell is not fraud to him, it is desecration. Ondine Marrach should say, for the first time, that her mother told her the Sharrow buoy was wrong two years ago and nobody at the Hall would enter it.

acts.title: Act 2: Taking the Buoy Apart
acts.description: The party salvages the northern Sharrow buoy and takes it to pieces, and finds inside it a bell that was cast from a stolen harbour bell of the Windward Beads. This act is investigative and physical in equal measure, and it produces the campaign's first piece of hard, portable, undeniable evidence.
objectives: Get a boat alongside a working bell-buoy in open water and get someone inside the cage
Recover the bell, or enough of it to prove what it is
Establish that the buoy has been moved and re-shackled within the last three months
Work out what the bell actually is, and where it came from

scenes.name: Alongside the Buoy
scenes.description: A boat, a swell, an iron cage weighing three tons swinging on a hundred fathoms of chain, and someone who has to get inside it. The most dangerous ten minutes in the scenario and there is nothing hostile within a mile.
scenes.readAloud: "Up close it is much bigger than it looked and much less friendly. The cage is cast iron, eight feet across, furred green with weed to the waterline and white with barnacle above it, and it does not ride the swell so much as get shoved through it, coming up out of a trough with four tons of momentum and a great deal of indifference to whatever is alongside. Inside the cage, on its frame, the bell swings and strikes and swings and strikes. The noise at three feet is not a sound. It is a physical event that happens to your skull. And Yevet Ourim, who has been staring at the cage since the boat came alongside, says: 'The paint. Look at the paint. That is three months old. Nobody has painted a Sounding buoy since the year of the short harvest.'"

skillChecks.success: You time the swell and get from the boat onto the cage and inside it, which is the sort of thing that looks like nothing and is worth telling people about for years.
skillChecks.failure: You go in the water between the boat and four tons of iron. 2d6 bludgeoning and a Strength save DC 13 or you are held under for a round; the crew get you out, and the second attempt is at advantage because you now know precisely how it wants to be done.

skillChecks.success: You hold the boat off the cage on an oar for the entire time somebody is inside, which is the actual heroic act in this scene, and nobody will ever mention it.
skillChecks.failure: The boat is stove along two strakes and takes water; everyone in it gets wet, cold and cross, and the jolly-boat is out of service for a day.

skillChecks.success: The signal pattern is not the pattern for the northern Sharrow. It is the pattern for a vessel in distress. This buoy has been re-set to ring a calling, permanently, into fog.
skillChecks.failure: It is very loud in here and you are trying not to be hit by a bell.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Play the buoy as a physical object with mass and no malice, and let the danger come entirely from that. If a player wants to solve this with a spell — Feather Fall, Misty Step, Spider Climb, Water Breathing, Enhance Ability — let them, generously; the party is levels 4 to 6 now and clever spell use should trivialise a physical obstacle occasionally. The evidence is the point, not the obstacle.
loot: The buoy's bell — 90 lb of recast bronze, and the single most important object in the campaign so far
The new shackle from the chain: smith's work, done ashore, stamped with a maker's mark

scenes.name: The Mark Under the Crown
scenes.description: The bell, on the deck of the Widow's Compass, in daylight, with the whole crew standing round it. The moment the campaign's central crime becomes a fact.
scenes.readAloud: "They get it in over the rail with a stay tackle and it lands on the deck with a noise that everybody feels in their back teeth, and then there is a lot of standing about looking at it, because a bell on a deck is a strange thing to be near. It has been recast, that much is obvious even to landsmen — the crown is rough where a fresh mould has taken badly, and there is a seam that no founder would leave. Anselm Coyle gets down on his knees beside it, which is not something anyone has seen him do, and puts his head under the lip and stays there a long time. When he comes out his face is wrong. He says, 'It's Nethercombe's.' Nobody says anything. He says, 'That's Nethercombe's harbour bell. I have rung it. I rang out my own father on it.'"

skillChecks.success: Half a harbour mark survives on the inside of the crown where the recasting did not take: a hamlet's bell-mark, and the founder's date beneath it. Anyone who knows the Beads can name it. Nethercombe, a Windward hamlet whose harbour bell vanished two years ago and was written off as theft for the metal.
skillChecks.failure: Rough bronze and a bad seam. You know it has been recast and you cannot say from what.

skillChecks.success: You know the story: three Beads hamlets lost their harbour bells in the same eighteen months, and all three were recorded at the Hall as metal theft, and none of the three has been able to afford a replacement since. A hamlet without a bell cannot ring a calling. A hamlet that cannot ring a calling is a hamlet nobody is obliged to answer for.
skillChecks.failure: Bells go missing. Bronze is worth money.

skillChecks.success: There is nothing magical about this bell whatsoever, and you should say so plainly to a party that is looking for a curse. It is metal, moved by people, for money. That is the whole of it and it is worse than a curse.
skillChecks.failure: You find nothing, which in this case is the correct answer arrived at unconvincingly.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Give Anselm Coyle this scene if a player is not running him, and give it to the player if they are. The theft of harbour bells is not vandalism in this setting: it is the removal of a hamlet's right to be rescued. Make sure that lands. Crew Regard +1 if the party's response is to promise the bell goes back to Nethercombe — and then hold them to it, because it is worth a great deal of money as metal and the ship is broke.
loot: Proof: 90 lb of bronze with half a stolen harbour's mark inside the crown
A maker's mark on the new shackle, traceable to a smith at Ambergrace

scenes.name: The Hall Will Not Look At It
scenes.description: The party takes the bell, or the evidence of it, to a Reckoner — and is refused. Not out of villainy: out of procedure, which is worse, and which the party cannot argue with.
scenes.readAloud: "You have ninety pounds of stolen bronze on a handcart in the middle of the Hall and the Reckoner on duty will not look at it. He is not being obstructive. He is being precise, which you are beginning to learn is the local dialect of obstruction. 'A buoy is the Hall's furniture,' he says. 'A complaint about the Hall's furniture is heard by the Hall in session. The Hall sits at the year's turn. You may enter a note.' Somebody says something about nine ships. He writes it down. He says, 'Entered.' And a clerk at the side table who has not looked up once in this entire conversation says, without stopping writing, and quite quietly: 'They will not sit on it. I wrote three of those entries myself and they have not sat on any of them.'"

skillChecks.success: You get the duty Reckoner to agree to a survey of the buoy's position at the Hall's expense. It will be conducted in nine weeks. He is being generous and both of you know it is useless.
skillChecks.failure: 'You may enter a note.' There is no version of this conversation that ends differently and the party should feel the wall.

skillChecks.success: The duty Reckoner is frightened. Not of you. He glanced twice at the door to the inner room while you were talking and he did not want to be having this conversation where he was having it.
skillChecks.failure: A clerk being a clerk.

skillChecks.success: The old clerk at the side table — thin as a page, sixty-something, writing steadily throughout — is Pellamy Doss, and he has just said something enormous in a very small voice. Follow it up.
skillChecks.failure: Somebody muttered something. The room is full of people muttering.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the scene that recruits Pellamy Doss (data/defaults/bellwater/npcs/pellamy-doss.json). He wrote three of the false marks against the Widow's Compass himself, and he was told to, and he has been waiting two years for somebody to walk into the Hall with a piece of bronze. He offers to sign on. He is sixty-eight, dying, and has budgeted his remaining months against the year's turn, and he does not mention any of that. The wall the party hits here is the campaign's real antagonist: not a villain, an institution that has been quietly bought and cannot be argued with from outside.
loot: Pellamy Doss, who signs the Articles the same evening and asks for a half share
Doss's copy of three ledger entries in his own hand, dated, positioned, and provably impossible

acts.title: Act 3: The Reef and the Quiet Folk
acts.description: The party dives the Sharrow, finds what is in the Charity Bell's forepeak, does right by it, and is met — because of that and only because of that — by the people who have been watching this reef for two years and were never asked a single question.
objectives: Dive the recent wrecks and establish that they were stripped by a crew with a method
Find the Charity Bell's slate and prove she was navigating to the false buoy when she died
Deal with the four dead in the forepeak under Article Six
Meet the quiet folk of Ossary Deep, and learn their count

scenes.name: Diving the Sharrow
scenes.description: Clear water, cold, and nine ships to look at. An exploration scene with genuine physical danger and no villain in it.
scenes.readAloud: "Going over the side into the Sharrow in flat calm at noon is the most beautiful thing that will happen to any of you this year, and you should all be aware that this is a horrible thing to be true. The water is the colour of a bottle held up to a window. The rock falls away in ledges and gullies, and lying along them, in that light, are the ships: a ketch on her side with her rigging still up and standing out sideways in the current like weed; a schooner broken across a shelf in two clean pieces; a small fat trader sitting almost upright in six fathoms as though she had been parked. Fish move through all of them without hurrying. And on every single one of them, where the copper and the bronze and the iron ought to be, there are bright clean cuts in the wood."

skillChecks.success: You work the shallow wrecks on held breath, efficiently, and come up unhurt. Repeat once per wreck; a character may attempt three dives before exhaustion enters it.
skillChecks.failure: You misjudge a swim-through and come up hard under an overhang: 1d6 bludgeoning and a level of exhaustion. A character at exhaustion 2 must stop diving for the day and everyone aboard will make sure they do.

skillChecks.success: The same tools, in the same order, on all nine: fastenings first, then instruments, then cargo. Two of the cuts still have bar-marks in them that match a pattern of bar you can describe to a smith. This is a crew with a list, working a reef they expect to keep working.
skillChecks.failure: They have been robbed. Everyone knows wrecks get robbed. You cannot show it is one crew rather than twenty.

skillChecks.success: You read the growth and date the wrecks against each other: nine ships in thirty-four months, spaced almost evenly. Nobody's bad luck is that regular.
skillChecks.failure: Weed is weed.

enemies: 1 giant octopus (in the after cabin of the Charity Bell, and only if its den is entered or robbed)
combatEncounters.tactics: The reef sharks are not a monster attack, they are wildlife, and they should be run that way: they circle, they close, they bump, and they will break off entirely if hurt once or if the party leaves the water. Give the party a round of warning — a shape at the limit of visibility — and let a successful Animal Handling or Nature check (DC 13) buy an orderly withdrawal with no fighting at all. The giant octopus will not initiate anything; it defends the after cabin of the Charity Bell and stops the instant it is left alone. Underwater combat rules apply: melee attacks with non-piercing weapons have disadvantage and ranged weapons other than crossbows have their normal range reduced to five feet. Characters without a swim speed or water breathing are on held breath and the round count matters.
combatEncounters.terrain: Four to eleven fathoms of open water over black rock, with wreck-timber, rigging and gullies for cover. Visibility forty feet. Any character who drops below zero hit points here drowns in three rounds unless someone gets them up.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The wildlife on the Sharrow is wildlife. If the party handles it well there is no fight, and a table that avoids both encounters entirely by being sensible has played this scene correctly and should be told so. The horror in this act is the bar-marks, not the sharks.
loot: About 200 gp of salvage the strippers left: cargo in the bilges, a brass-cased chronometer under a sprung deck, a chest of coin in a locked cabin nobody thought worth opening
The Charity Bell's slate, with a course and a bearing to the northern Sharrow buoy chalked on it four hours before she died

scenes.name: The Forepeak of the Charity Bell
scenes.description: Four people in the smallest compartment of a small ship, seven months down, where they went to get away from the water. Handle this scene with restraint and let it be quiet.
scenes.readAloud: "The forepeak of a ketch is a triangle about the size of a large cupboard and it is the highest part of the hull when she goes down by the stern, and that is why people go there. The door is shut from the inside. There is no need to describe what is in it beyond this: there are four of them, and they are together, and one of them is small. On the deckhead above them, where somebody could reach it lying on their back in the dark, somebody has scratched four names into the paint with a knife, in order, taking their time over it, and the last one is unfinished."

skillChecks.success: You get the names off the deckhead. All four, though the last is only three letters. That is enough to ring them out properly and enough to write to somebody in the Beads.
skillChecks.failure: You cannot make the last two out, and Anselm Coyle will spend two hours in the water going back for them, and get them.

scenes.roleplayNotes: No rolls to hit, no horror, no undead, no twist. This is the campaign's tone floor doing its job: deaths at sea are given weight and not dwelt on. Article Six now applies — the dead are named and rung out before the ship sails on — and honouring it costs the party the best part of a day on a reef in an exposed anchorage. The crew will not regard that as a question. If the party tries to sail without doing it, Article Six's restitution is exactly as written: the ship comes about and it is done properly, whatever it costs, and Crew Regard drops by 2. If the party does it without being pushed, Crew Regard +1. Ring them out on the recast Nethercombe bell, which is what makes the next scene happen.
loot: A child's brass whistle on a lanyard, which should be returned to the Beads and not sold

scenes.name: The Count in Bronze
scenes.description: The quiet folk of Ossary Deep come up to the edge of the drop-off, because somebody finally rang a bell over this reef for a reason that was not money. First contact, on their terms.
scenes.readAloud: "You ring the four of them out at sunset, off the seaward face where the reef drops away, using the stolen bell because it is the only bell you have and because it seems right that it should do one honest thing. Anselm says the names. The last note is still in the air when the water under the counter goes dark — not shadowed, dark, the way a cloud crosses a field — and then there are tones coming up out of a hundred fathoms. Not one bell. Nine or ten, struck in sequence, patterned, answering. Something comes up the face of the drop-off at a speed that no swimmer manages, stops eight feet down, and looks at you: grey as a wet stone, wide-eyed, with a bronze bar across her back and a collar of small hammered bells at her throat, and she strikes two of them with a knuckle, twice, and waits. Sefi Nightjar, nineteen years old and never off the chain in her life, says, 'Captain, I think she's counting.'"

skillChecks.success: She is not threatening and she is not curious. She is angry, and the anger is old and specific, and it is not aimed at you. She has come up because of the bell you rang, and she is here to tell you a number.
skillChecks.failure: A deepwater person eight feet under your counter, striking bells, and no way at all to read her face.

skillChecks.success: You answer her on the bell. Badly — but you answer, in tone and rhythm, and that is the entire protocol of her people. She strikes back, slower, teaching. This is how the party learns anything from the quiet folk for the rest of the campaign.
skillChecks.failure: You make a noise. She waits, patiently, in the way that makes it clear the noise was not an answer.

skillChecks.success: Along the reef face at the lip of the drop-off, set into the rock, there is a line of small hammered bronze markers. Fourteen of them. The party has counted nine wrecks. The quiet folk have counted fourteen, because five of the ships that died over this reef were carried off the ledge into deep water and were never found and never entered in any ledger anywhere.
skillChecks.failure: Something bronze on the reef face, catching the last light. You will need to come back for it.

scenes.roleplayNotes: THE QUIET FOLK ARE AN ORIGINAL PEOPLE OF THIS SETTING. They are not tritons, not sahuagin, not kuo-toa, not merfolk, and the DM should not play them as any of those, describe them with any of those words, or reach for any of those stat blocks. They are a deepwater bronze-working nation who speak by striking tones, who keep a scrupulous count of who has answered a calling and who has not, and who have been watching ships die on the Sharrow for two years without ever being asked a single question by anyone from the surface. That last fact is the point of the scene and it should land as an accusation, gently and without a speech. Ledda (data/defaults/bellwater/npcs/ledda-of-ossary.json) is the one who comes up, and she joins the party after this scenario, not before. At first the party understands her only in fragments — give them a third of what she says, and let Performance and time close the gap over the following sessions.
loot: The count: fourteen, not nine. Five unrecorded wrecks in deep water off the Sharrow's seaward face
Ledda of Ossary, who comes aboard after this scenario
A hammered bronze marker, given, which the quiet folk will recognise anywhere on the chain

npcsInvolved.name: Ledda of Ossary
npcsInvolved.role: Quiet Folk of Ossary Deep / Companion from the end of this scenario
npcsInvolved.description: Grey as a wet stone, wide-eyed, with a bronze bar across her back and a collar of small hammered bells at her throat that she strikes to speak. She is a druid of a deepwater tradition that has nothing to do with forests, and she has been keeping the count on the Sharrow's face for two years. Full file at data/defaults/bellwater/npcs/ledda-of-ossary.json.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Somebody must be made to answer for fourteen ships. She came up because a bell was rung honestly over this reef for the first time in her memory, and she has decided to find out whether that means anything.

npcsInvolved.name: Pellamy Doss
npcsInvolved.role: Retired Reckoners' clerk / Companion from Act 2
npcsInvolved.description: Sixty-eight, thin as a page, and the quietest person in any room he is in. He wrote three of the false marks against the Widow's Compass with his own hand because he was told to, and he has been waiting two years for somebody to walk into the Hall with a piece of evidence. He signs the Articles the evening he meets the party and asks for a half share. Full file at data/defaults/bellwater/npcs/pellamy-doss.json.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To put right three entries in a book. He is dying, he has budgeted his remaining months against the year's turn, and he mentions none of this to anyone.

npcsInvolved.name: Duty Reckoner Ivo Sarn
npcsInvolved.description: Correct, procedural, and frightened. He will not look at the bell, he will enter a note, and he glances twice at the inner door while doing it. He is not on the Hollow Bell's books himself; he simply knows which of his colleagues are and has decided that is not his business.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To finish his shift without having had this conversation.

npcsInvolved.name: Anselm Coyle
npcsInvolved.role: Bell-priest of the Sounding / Party member or NPC
npcsInvolved.description: If no player is running him, run him hard in this scenario: he is the character for whom a false bell is not fraud but desecration, and the recast Nethercombe bell nearly breaks him. He rang out his own father on that bell. Full file at data/defaults/bellwater/characters/anselm-coyle.json.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The Sounding is holy or his entire life is a mistake, and he has just been handed ninety pounds of evidence for the second option.

npcsInvolved.name: Ondine Marrach
npcsInvolved.description: This is the scenario where she becomes useful to the party rather than an obstacle to them: her mother told her two years ago that the Sharrow buoy was wrong, and told the Hall, and the Hall entered a note. She has been carrying that and nobody has ever believed her. Full file at data/defaults/bellwater/npcs/ondine-marrach.json.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To be told, by somebody, that her mother was not a coward.

rewards.gold: Approximately 340 gp in shares after the ledger count — about 200 gp of salvage the strippers left on the Sharrow, a 60 gp brass-cased chronometer, and 80 gp of coin from a cabin nobody had thought worth opening. The recast Nethercombe bell is worth 90 gp as metal and should not be sold.
items: The false bell of the northern Sharrow buoy — recast bronze, 90 lb, with half of Nethercombe's harbour mark surviving inside the crown. The campaign's first hard evidence
The re-shackle from the buoy chain, smith's work, bearing a maker's mark from Ambergrace
The Charity Bell's slate: a course and bearing to the false buoy, chalked four hours before she sank
A brass-cased chronometer in working order (60 gp) — genuinely useful for the ship's navigation and worth keeping
Pellamy Doss's copies of three ledger entries in his own hand, dated and provably impossible
A hammered bronze marker of the quiet folk, given as a token and recognised anywhere on the chain
rewards.story: The party has proof that false bells exist, that harbour bells have been stolen from Beads hamlets and recast to make them, and that the Sharrow has killed nine ships in three years — or fourteen, by a count nobody at the Hall has ever asked for. They also have a Reckoners' clerk who wrote three of their own false marks, a deepwater nation that is now watching them specifically, and no institution on the chain willing to look at any of it. The ship is slower than she was, needs a yard, and cannot get one on the windward side. Ambergrace is the only place that will careen a nine-marked hull.

twists: The calling is real bronze and a real signal and there is no ship. The trap is not magical and not clever; it is a stolen bell, re-hung, ringing distress into fog forever, and it works because the Sounding requires people to answer bells.

The buoy was moved. The chain has been re-shackled within three months with smith's work done ashore, which means the false calling is maintained — somebody comes out here on a schedule to keep the trap in good order.

The Reckoners' Hall will not look at ninety pounds of stolen bronze standing in the middle of its own floor. Not from corruption in the moment, but from procedure: the Hall sits at the year's turn. The party's evidence is entered as a note, and Pellamy Doss says out loud, quietly, that he wrote three such entries himself and nothing was ever done.

The quiet folk's count is fourteen, not nine. Five ships went over the ledge into deep water and were never found, never reported, and never entered in any ledger. Nobody has ever asked them anything.

One of the three ledger entries Pellamy Doss wrote against the Widow's Compass concerns a calling from the Sharrow — which means Idony Marrach was here, heard this bell, knew it was false, and sailed on. The party is now standing where she stood, having very nearly died proving her right.
dmTips: THE CENTRAL RULE OF THIS SCENARIO: no monster caused any of this. The bell is metal, the buoy was moved by people in a boat, the ships were stripped with iron bars by a crew working a list. If a player casts Detect Magic on the bell, the correct answer is nothing, and it should be given plainly. The campaign's dread is economic and the moment it becomes supernatural it stops working.

THE QUIET FOLK ARE ORIGINAL TO THIS SETTING. Not tritons, not sahuagin, not kuo-toa, not merfolk. Do not use those names, those descriptions or those stat blocks. They are grey, wide-eyed, bronze-working deepwater people who speak by striking tones and keep a count of who answers callings. If you need mechanics for one in a fight — and you should try very hard not to need any — build from a druid or a scout and give them a swim speed, and describe them as themselves.

GIVE THE PARTY ONLY A THIRD OF WHAT LEDDA SAYS AT FIRST. Bell-tone is a real language and the party does not speak it. Narrate fragments — a number, a direction, an emotion — and let Performance checks, time aboard, and Yevet Ourim's notebooks close the gap over the following two scenarios. Do not hand over a translator.

ARTICLE SIX IS THE HINGE OF ACT 3. Four dead in the forepeak, and ringing them out costs the best part of a day at an exposed anchorage on a reef. Let the crew be immovable about it. Then have the quiet folk come up because of it — not as a reward the party earned, which would cheapen it, but as a consequence: somebody finally rang a bell over this reef for a reason that was not money, and they came to see who.

IF THE SHIP TOUCHED IN ACT 1, THAT DAMAGE IS PERMANENT UNTIL A YARD FIXES IT. Two feet of water, a sprung plank forward, pumps manned every watch. Say so at the time, put it in world state, and let it be the reason the party has to go to Ambergrace in bw-scenario-003. If they got off clean, the fouled bottom alone is enough reason — she is two knots slow and cannot outrun anything.

PELLAMY DOSS RECRUITS HIMSELF and the party should barely notice it happening. He says one sentence at a side table, follows them out, and asks for a half share. Do not have him explain himself. His confession that he wrote three of the marks comes out over the following week, in pieces, unprompted, and he never asks to be forgiven for it.

DO NOT LET THE PARTY WIN AT THE HALL. Act 2's third scene must end in refusal. The wall is the campaign's real antagonist — an institution partly bought and entirely procedural — and the party needs to feel that no amount of evidence carried through the front door will move it. That is what makes bw-scenario-004's public reckoning at the year's turn mean anything.

TRACK CREW REGARD. Natural movements in this scenario: promising the Nethercombe bell goes home (+1); ringing out the four without being pushed (+1); taking salvage before the count, which somebody will be tempted to do on the Sharrow (Article Two, -1); sailing from the Charity Bell without the naming (Article Six, -2, and the ship comes about anyway).

PACE IT AS FOUR SESSIONS: the calling and the near-wreck; the buoy and the bell; the Hall and Pellamy Doss; the reef, the forepeak and the quiet folk. The dive should be its own session and should feel like a holiday for about ten minutes before it stops being one.

IF THE PARTY REFUSES THE CALLING IN ACT 1 on suspicion, run it. No mark is entered because no vessel was in distress; Crew Regard drops 1 for ignoring bronze and rises 2 when the proof arrives; and the scenario reaches the same reef by a different road, with the party arriving in daylight and much less frightened. That is a fair reward for cleverness and it costs the scenario nothing.
